extracted.intended_audience: factory owners, plant managers, and industrial employers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for operating high-capacity, humane, and profitable factories, covering workplace safety, shop layout, ventilation, machine safeguarding, wage systems, profit-sharing, and business stability. Aimed at employers who manage production and labour policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean, well-lighted, well-ventilated factory
rubrics_metrics.description: One point that is absolutely essential to high capacity, as well as to humane production, is a clean, well-lighted and well-ventilated factory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep nearly even temperature year-round; provide sufficient daylight so artificial light is unnecessary during daylight; detail staff to keep shops clean, wash windows, refresh paint; paint dark corners white to discourage expectoration. 'One cannot have morale without cleanliness.' Tolerate no makeshift cleanliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific machine placement and measured floor-space per job
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines are scientifically arranged to give every man and every machine every square inch that he requires and, if possible, not a square inch, and certainly not a square foot, more than he requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure on each job the exact amount of room a man needs; place machines close together to reduce overhead and transport costs while ensuring no worker is cramped. Close placement requires maximum safeguards and ventilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machines must be absolutely safe (machine safeguarding)
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not consider any machine--no matter how efficiently it may turn out its work--as a proper machine unless it is absolutely safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test new machines in every way before installation; trace every accident no matter how trivial with a skilled investigator and study the machine to make the same accident impossible in the future. Make machinery 'fool-proof' where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic accident investigation and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Every accident, no matter how trivial, is traced back by a skilled man employed solely for that purpose, and a study is made of the machine to make that same accident in the future impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dedicated personnel for accident tracing; categorize principal causes of accidents and address them systematically; prioritize preventing mental states that invite accidents (overwork, fatigue), preventing carelessness, and engineering safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address principal causes of accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal causes of accidents as they are grouped by the experts are: (1) Defective structures; (2) defective machines; (3) insufficient room; (4) absence of safeguards; (5) unclean conditions; (6) bad lights; (7) bad air; (8) unsuitable clothing; (9) carelessness; (10) ignorance; (11) mental condition; (12) lack of cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many of these (defective structures/machines, insufficient room, unclean conditions, bad light/air, wrong mental condition, lack of cooperation) can be solved by design, wages, and construction. Guard specifically against unsuitable clothing, carelessness, and ignorance with supervision, training, and engineering controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard belts and older power-transmission hazards; prefer individual motors
rubrics_metrics.description: In all of our new construction, each machine has its individual electric motor, but in the older construction we had to use belts. Every belt is guarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conveyors create crossing hazards, place bridges so no man has to cross at a dangerous point. Ensure there are no open parts of machines where clothing can be caught; keep aisles clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect workers from flying debris and hot surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever there is a possibility of flying metal, the workman is required to wear goggles and the chances are further reduced by surrounding the machine with netting. Around hot furnaces we have railings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce PPE (goggles) and add physical barriers (netting, railings) as engineering controls to reduce risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control machine start/operation to prevent thoughtless activation
rubrics_metrics.description: The starting switches of draw presses are protected by big red tags which have to be removed before the switch can be turned--this prevents the machine being started thoughtlessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interlocks, tags, or other protective devices to require intentional actions before machines can be started; design controls to reduce inadvertent operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervise and control unsuitable clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Workmen will wear unsuitable clothing--ties that may be caught in a pulley, flowing sleeves, and all manner of unsuitable articles. The bosses have to watch for that, and they catch most of the offenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foremen should monitor clothing and enforce suitable work attire to reduce entanglement risks; combine supervision with machine guards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive hours and mental fatigue to reduce accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man has worked too hard or through too long hours he gets into a mental state that invites accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage workloads and hours; reduce overwork to prevent mental states that invite accidents. Wages and working hours adjustments are part of accident prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation and building design to support health
rubrics_metrics.description: In all the later buildings, the supporting columns are made hollow and through them the bad air is pumped out and the good air introduced. A nearly even temperature is kept everywhere the year round and, during daylight, there is nowhere the necessity for artificial light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate ventilation into structural design (e.g., hollow columns), maintain even temperatures, and design for natural light where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of time studies and job standardization for fair wage rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting about 1913 we had time studies made of all the thousands of operations in the shops... By the time figures all of the jobs in our factory were standardized and rates set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct time studies to determine theoretical outputs, make allowances to set a satisfactory standard output for a day, and set rates that express skill and exertion required; avoid wage inequities caused by guesswork.

rubrics_metrics.name: No piece work; require a fixed day's standard output
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not have piece work. Some of the men are paid by the day and some are paid by the hour, but in practically every case there is a required standard output below which a man is not expected to fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a required standard output for each job; pay workers for presence and for work with a clear minimum standard so both employer and employee know whether wages are earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum wage and profit-sharing tied to performance and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In January, 1914, a kind of profit-sharing plan in which the minimum wage for any class of work and under certain conditions was five dollars a day... The plan was to distribute profits, but instead of waiting until the profits had been earned--to approximate them in advance and to add them, under certain conditions, to the wages of those persons who had been in the employ of the company for six months or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine a guaranteed minimum with periodic profit additions credited to hourly rates to favor lower-paid workers; tie eligibility to service duration and to non-production conditions (initially: home/cleanliness/citizenship standards), but be aware of paternalism and adjust methods to avoid prying into private lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification-based eligibility for bonus sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: It was classified participation among three classes of employees: (1) Married men living with and taking good care of their families. (2) Single men over twenty-two years of age who are of proved thrifty habits. (3) Young men under twenty-two years of age, and women who are the sole support of some next of kin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design eligibility classes to reflect social/household responsibilities; the plan credited profit-sharing to hourly rates and paid every two weeks to provide immediate incentive, but monitor for unintended paternalistic administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie bonuses to present-day performance rather than deferred charity
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection to [previous profit-sharing] plan was that it had no direct connection with the day's work. A man did not get his share until long after his work was done and then it came to him almost in the way of a present. It is always unfortunate to have wages tinged with charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure profit-sharing so rewards are closely tied in time and amount to the worker's actual performance to avoid perceptions of charity and to provide effective incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid paternalism in welfare/bonus-on-conduct schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: There were objections to the bonus-on-conduct method of paying wages. It tended toward paternalism. Paternalism has no place in industry. Welfare work that consists in prying into employees' private concerns is out of date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide counsel and help for decency's sake but redesign social-welfare measures to avoid prying into private life; prefer investment/participation plans that solidify industry rather than conduct-based penalties/bonuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of raising wages without raising production
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a danger in too rapidly raising the pay of any man--... The thought of easy money breaks down work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure wage increases are supported by higher production; otherwise increased pay can reduce motivation/performance. Use incentives that encourage increased output and skill, not just higher pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix wages so employees have no financial worries
rubrics_metrics.description: If you expect a man to give his time and energy, fix his wages so that he will have no financial worries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set wage levels that remove basic financial anxiety so workers can concentrate on giving their best. Evidence presented: reduced turnover and higher retention when wages are stabilized and sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: View employer-worker relation as partnership
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a man finds the production part of a business too much for his own time or strength, he calls in assistants to share the management with him... The boss is the partner of his worker, the worker is partner of his boss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame labour relations around reciprocal dependence and shared goals; both sides should avoid assuming indispensability and should work to make the business profitable so wages can rise sustainably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business limits wages; manage business to increase capacity for wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The business itself sets the limits. You cannot distribute $150,000 out of a business that brings in only $100,000. The business limits the wages, but does anything limit the business? The business limits itself by following bad precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than demanding higher wages abstractly, focus on stimulating and managing the business so it can pay higher wages. Avoid actions (strikes, lockouts) that can 'assassinate' a business and harm all dependents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages should cover worker's outside obligations and future (old age)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wage carries all the worker's obligations outside the shop; it carries all that is necessary in the way of service and management inside the shop... And certainly it ought to be made to take care of the worker's sunset days when labour is no longer possible to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider components such as family support, housing, education, and old-age provision (pensions). Recognize the difficulty of computing exact requirements but aim to structure wages and benefits to meet these obligations rather than leaving them to charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: High wages begin with shop production and honest work
rubrics_metrics.description: The high wage begins down in the shop. If it is not created there it cannot get into pay envelopes... The kind of workman who gives the business the best that is in him is the best kind of workman a business can have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate workmanship, honest effort, and effective management in the shop as the starting point for sustainable higher wages. Reward higher production with pay increases tied to productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paying good wages is profitable and reduces turnover
rubrics_metrics.description: If you expect a man to give his time and energy, fix his wages so that he will have no financial worries. It pays. Our profits, after paying good wages and a bonus... show that paying good wages is the most profitable way of doing business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented benefits: drastic reduction in hiring/higher retention; example: turnover fell from needing 53,000 hires per year to ~6,508 after wage plan. Use wage policy as long-term investment in stability and goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reshape business on basis of service to stabilize booms and busts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is wholly desirable to reshape business on the basis of service. Then a better financial system will have to come... The periodic depressions are more serious because they seem so vast as to be uncontrollable. Until the whole reorganization is brought about, they cannot be wholly controlled, but each man in business can easily do something for himself...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage production, financing, and product mix with the aim of service to reduce seasonal and cyclical volatility; consider plant location and product scheduling to complement farming or seasonal cycles and to 'iron out' seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate and organize plants to complement farming and seasonal work
rubrics_metrics.description: By the use of machinery farming need not consume more than a fraction of the time it now consumes... We established [a plant] eighteen miles out in the country so that the workers could also be farmers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider locating operations where employees can supplement incomes through farming or arrange production so seasonal industries have complementary schedules; use machinery to reduce total labor time required for agriculture enabling dual occupations.
